en: Oṃ.
Homage to the glorious Supreme Self.
Now, salutation to the Self-abiding God, the eternal, whose sins are destroyed, who has abandoned all sequential divisions, and who is the light of pure consciousness. 1.

At the conclusion of the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager speaks: "Today, indeed, during the festival of the Blessed Lord Kālapriyanātha, the noble gentlemen have commanded that [this play] be performed, in which there is the intense exertion of a great man—profound and terrifying—and in which the speech is both pleasing and harsh, yet rich in meaning. (2)
In extraordinary vessels, the aesthetic flavor (rasa) in which the Hero resides is divided according to each respective substratum through subtle, manifested distinctions. //3//
"That composition is to be performed.
(With joy: "In effect, it has been commanded that the *Mahāvīracarita* is to be staged," and so forth.
For the poetry of a poet whose speech is mastered, and the narrative which has Rāma as its subject—these two [are now joined].
And people have obtained a touchstone for testing the flow of his speech. //4//

Thus do I inform you: there is a city named Padmapura in the southern region (Dakṣiṇāpatha). Therein dwell certain followers of the Taittirīya school, belonging to the lineage of Kaśyapa, who are teachers of the Caraṇas, purifiers of the assembly, maintainers of the five sacred fires, observers of vows, drinkers of Soma, those named Udumbara, and exponents of the Veda.

Let your honors know that we have as our friend a poet named Bhavabhūti—the son of Jātūkarṇī; the grandson of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Gopāla, who was a great poet of auspicious name and a performer of the Vājapeya sacrifice; and the biological son of Nīlakaṇṭha, whose fame is pure; and who bears the title Śrīkaṇṭha.
He is the best among the supreme ascetics (paramahaṃsas), like Aṅgiras among the great seers (maharṣis). His venerable guru is a treasury of knowledge whose name is true to his nature. (5)

Thus, out of a love for the heroic and the marvelous, this life-story of the Joy of the Raghus—the subduer of those who harm righteousness—has been composed; it is wonderful, possessing great heroism and boldness, and it has uprooted the very source of the world's triple affliction.

Therefore, may you gentlemen complete this work. And it was said by that son of a Vedic scholar: "The sage Pracetasa, the bull among sages and the foremost of poets, composed that purifying narrative of the Lord of the Raghus;
may virtuous men, with well-pleased minds, enjoy those words of mine as well, for I too am devoted to it. (7)

(Entering, the actor says: The members of the assembly have been propitiated; however, because this composition is unprecedented, they wish to know the subject matter of the narrative at its commencement.

The Stage Manager: That Blessed One, Viśvāmitra of the Kauśika clan, who was about to undergo initiation, went to the house of Daśaratha—the royal seer of the Ikṣvāku line whose family priest was Vasiṣṭha—and having returned to his own penance grove, he brought with him Prince Rāma, accompanied by his younger brother. This was done so that Rāma might manifest his innate prowess through weapons, which is the seed for the welfare of the world; so that he might obtain Maithilī, the source of benefit for the universe; and so that he might become a worthy vessel for the glorious and auspicious feat of destroying the race of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa. (8)
Having been invited by him, that lord of Videha, having already undertaken the consecration, dispatched his brother;
this very king named Kuśadhvaja is approaching together with Sītā and Urmilā. (9)
(Thus they both exit. //The Prologue//

(Then enter the King seated in a chariot, along with the charioteer and the two maidens. King: Long-lived Sītā and Ūrmilā, today the venerable Viśvāmitra is to be saluted by you two with a heart full of faith.
Daughter, do as your younger brother commands.
The King said: "For he is indeed the fourth sacred fire, or perhaps the fifth Veda;
or else he is a moving place of pilgrimage, or Dharma itself walking in embodied form. (10)

Sūta: O Lord of Sāṅkāśya, it is even so. Indeed, no one else excels the greatness of the seer Viśvāmitra. Those who know the traditional narratives recount his immeasurable collection of wonders, such as the *Traiśaṅkava*, the *Śaunaḥśepha*, and the paralyzing of Rambhā. Therefore, toward this preceptor—who has attained peace through the prayers of Brahmā and the other gods and sages, who is a repository of the splendor of ascetic power, and who has himself offered the Veda—only you are praiseworthy in this world as a householder among those with families, for you have made your home a dwelling place of the sciences. (11)
The King: Excellent, O charioteer, excellent! You speak indeed with truth. For these venerable great seers have realized Brahman; their association brings about a future of supreme auspiciousness.

Darkness is dispelled, tranquility increases greatly, and even from a single conversation, prosperity spreads both in this world and the next. Furthermore, their very presence bestows an indescribable majesty, and the words of those who are gracious produce immeasurable fruit. (12)

Charioteer: There is seen that hermitage of the sage, named Siddhāśramapada, delightful with forests in its green surroundings and encircled by the Kauśikī river. What need of more? It is that very son of Kuśika, accompanied by two others, who has come out to meet you.
The King: If it is so, let us alight from the chariot.
(Having descended with the two maidens: Charioteer, let the soldiers be told that no one is to tread upon the grounds in the vicinity of the hermitage.
Sūta: As you command.
(Thus he exits.
(Then Viśvāmitra enters, along with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. Viśvāmitra:
(To himself:

On this auspicious day, the rites for warding off demons and ensuring prosperity must be performed for the marriage of Vaidehī and the scion of Raghu; likewise, the entry into initiation must be undertaken by us skilled ones.
Furthermore, those various wondrous deeds of the enemy of the Daityas, who has Rāma as his soul, must be established for the welfare of the worlds; thus, being truly busily occupied, we rejoice. (13)

And a message was sent by us to the royal sage of Mithilā, saying: "According to custom, you are invited as a sacrificer to the sacrifice; however, Kuśadhvaja must be sent along with Sītā and Urmilā. And this was done by our dear friend.
The two princes said: "Blessed One, who is this great-souled Putana, before whom even you, O Venerable Ones, have thus risen?"
Viśvāmitra: It is well known that there were royal sages born of the lineage of Nimi among the Videhas;
their heir today is the aged King Sīradhvaja, to whom the sage Yājñavalkya recited the complete study of the Brahman.
The two princes said: "In whose house that bow of Maheśvara is worshipped."
Viśvāmitra: Indeed so.
The two princes:
(With curiosity) Now, it is said that there was yet another marvel there, namely, that the maiden was not born from a womb.
Viśvāmitra: (Laughing) That indeed exists;
however, this is the house of one who is about to perform a sacrifice for me, the sacrificer.
Out of affection for him, he dispatched his younger brother, Kuśadhvaja.
Therefore, O Vatsas, you must behave with humility toward this king who is learned in the Vedas.
The two princes: "So be it.
The King: (Gazing at them)
"By their very nature, these two possess marks of merit; indeed, this is known: they are surely the sons of a king who have already received the initiation ceremony. (16)
Oh, how beautiful is the form of this second caste and first stage of life, as well as of this fresh youth! (17)
For thus he is:
on his back he carries two quivers whose heron-feathered arrows kiss his top-knot, and his chest bears the skin of a ruru deer marked with a small smear of holy ashes.
He is girt with a girdle of *maurva* grass and wears a crimson lower garment; in his hand he holds a bow, a rosary, and a ring, while his other staff is made of *pippala* wood. //18//
Maiden, these people are indeed pleasant to behold.
The King: (Approaching) Venerable sir, I salute you.

Viśvāmitra: By good fortune, I see you, appearing as a young boy, arrived safely from the house of the royal sage. Therefore, embrace me. (Embracing him) Is that lord of Videha well, and has his sacrifice proceeded successfully?
And Gautama Śatānanda was the family priest of the Janakas.
The King: Indeed, noble sir, he alone is happy together with his family priest Dairghatapasas, for whose sake you all have thus followed the conduct of a household.
O maiden, we pay homage.
The King:
These two who have emerged so beautifully from the sacrificial ground as it is being furrowed by the plow are Sītā and this second daughter of Janaka, Ūrmilā. (20)
Viśvāmitra: May it be well with you.
Lakṣmaṇa:
(Aside) Noble brother, this noble lady is the mother of a wonder.
Rāma: [Listens.]
Her birth was from the sacrificial ground of the gods; her father is a king who speaks the Veda;
and her form is so serene and radiant that it inspires affection in me. (21)
The King: Blessed One, who are these two Kṣatriya religious students following you, appearing as if they have risen up, placing righteousness before them, with their majesty and prowess? (22)
Viśvāmitra; the two sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
The two princes:
(Approaching with humility) O Teacher, we salute you.
The King: By good fortune, the offspring of the great king Daśaratha is seen! (Embracing them) The birth of these two children could not have been possible except from the lineage of the Raghavas.
Apart from the ocean of milk, whence could the birth of the moon and the Kaustubha gem have occurred? //23//
Indeed, this nectar for our ears has been heard by us before:
that the sons of the Lord of Kosala, who possess the glory of merit, have been recovered with great difficulty through the ministrations of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga;
they, all four of them, desiring to reach the further shore of radiant spiritual welfare, are practicing the life of celibacy. (24)
Therefore, we pray for the continued well-being of your honors. Indeed, the excellence of the Raghu lineage is already established;
for whom the venerable son of Mitrāvaruṇa [Vasiṣṭha] prescribes the rites purified by the Vedas, and in whom resides the exclusive duty of protecting the people.
In the most exalted lineage of King Sāvitra Manu, the majesty of you kings—who have attained the Self—is never within the range of words or the intellect. 25.
Viśvāmitra:
You alone are capable of praising them—those whose meritorious deeds were untiring, whose fame is for the most part purifying, and who possess knowledge of their own great magnanimity. (26)
"Friend, having rested, worldly people enter into dwellings; therefore, let us sit for a moment here in the shade of this *vikaṅkata* tree."
(Thus they walk around and sit down.
(Offstage: Victory, victory, O Lord of the World! O Rāmacandra, victory!
(All gaze on with wonder.
The King: Blessed One, who indeed is this deity?

Viśvāmitra said: "There was a wife of the great ṛṣi Gautama Autathya named Ahalyā, from whom Śatānanda Āṅgirasa was born. Indra lusted after her; therefore, they designate him as 'the leaper upon Gautama’s wife' and 'the paramour of Ahalyā. Then the Blessed One became filled with wrath; he directed his sin toward her in the form of the blinding darkness (*andhatāmisra*). Today, this very woman has been liberated from that impurity by the splendor of Rāmabhadra."
The King: How is it that this dear son, the prince Vaikartana, possesses such immeasurable innate majesty and power?
Sītā:
(Gazing with affectionate longing and aside) His demeanor is truly in keeping with his physical form.
The King: [Listens.]
(Sighing:
Sītā would indeed have been given to Rāma, the moon among the sons of Daśaratha, who possesses a glorious splendor worthy of her;
had he not made the stringing of the bow of Tryambaka a non-negotiable wager. (27)
(Entering) An aged Rākṣasa named Sarvamāya, the priest of Rāvaṇa, has arrived; he has indeed come here on royal business and wishes to see you.
O maiden! Hūṃ, a rākṣasa!
The two princes: A source of great curiosity!
King Viśvāmitra:
(Reflecting) Let him come.
(The ascetic exits.
(Entering, Rākṣasa:
The Ten-faced one was forbidden from taking [her] by force by his maternal grandfather Mālyavat.
He sent me to the capital city of the King of Mithilā to choose as his bride a princess not born from a womb. //28//
And there I saw that king, the sacrificer; at his word, I followed after Kauśika and Kuśadhvaja.
(Thus they walk around.
Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa: (To Sītā and Ūrmilā respectively; to themselves: Why does this [woman] refresh my eyes like a wick of nectar?
Sītā and Urmilā: (Toward them both) Why does my sight, which brings joy to my eyes, linger upon these two?
Rākṣasa: (Approaching and seeing her) This is that Sītā of supernatural form! It was only right that the King should exert such effort. Homage to you! Is the King in good health?
The two [said]: "Welcome; please be seated here."
Is it well with your lord, he whose command Indra—the subduer of Pāka—honors by bowing his head, even as his crown slips from it? (29)
The Rākṣasa:
(Approaching) Is it well with my lord? And this is what the Great King has commanded you:
"A jewel of a maiden, born not from a womb, belongs to you; and we are seekers of such a jewel. For wherever a jewel exists, it may be obtained by us even from Śakra himself."

For it is considered that the maiden's purpose is solely for the sake of another; by giving her away, I shall become your kinsman, as will Pulastya, Pulaha, and the foremost of the others, who shall be our relatives.
Sītā: Alas, alas! A Rākṣasa is pursuing me!
Ūrmilā: Alas! How can this be so?
(The King and Viśvāmitra reflect. Lakṣmaṇa:
(Aside) Noble brother, noble brother, do you not see that the lord of the night-stalkers is making advances for this lady?
Rāma:
Child, even another might ask for a maiden without fear because of her common status;
how much more so the conqueror of the worlds, the great-grandson of the Supreme Lord? (31)

Lakṇamaṇa: Out of extreme benevolence, my noble brother feels great respect even for that night-stalker who is by nature our enemy—he who, through the destruction of the three Vedas, diminishes our kṣatriya splendor, and who, it is said, slew the Ikṣvāku royal sage Anaraṇya. (32)

Rāma: Granted, an enemy may deserve to be slain; however, you ought not to designate one who possesses immeasurable ascetic power, who is exceedingly heroic, and who is extraordinary, as if he were an ordinary man.
Lakṣmaṇa: What heroism is there in one who has cast aside the conduct of a brave man?
Rāma: Child, do not say such a thing!
That even one so learned and of such noble lineage should stray from the path of dharma—what can we say to that? It is simply another matter; all virtues do not reside in one place.
Who else is such a hero as the venerable descendant of Jamadagni, who effortlessly conquered the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) and achieved universal victory without obstacle? (33)
Rākṣasa: Oh, sir! Why is this being deliberated?

Let the daughter of the Earth rest upon the chest of that world-conqueror—[a chest] radiant with the knots of healed wounds inlaid with fragments of thunderbolts shattered by a sudden impact; [a chest] where the tusks of the formidable elephant Indra were once broken; [and a chest] which serves as a garland of flowers fashioned by the goddess of Nandana for her lord—just as the Fortune of Heroes rests there. (34)
(A confused clamor behind the scenes.

King: Holy sir, since these great sages, invited to the sacrifice, are arriving from all directions with their sons and wives, it is for this very reason that there is this confused clamor filled with cries of lamentation.
(All rise. Lakṣmaṇa: But who is this woman, filling the sky with the sounds of her many swaying ornaments—mostly large skulls strung with entrails and armlets that jingle harshly?

With a body made terrifying by the weight of her swaying, trembling breasts—which are like a dense, formidable mountain slope of mud consisting of blood she has drunk and vomited—she runs with haughty strides. //35//
Viśvāmitra:
This is the daughter of Suketu and the wife of the asura Sunda;
she is the formidable Rākṣasī named Tāṭakā, the mother of Mārīca. (36)
Daughter, those wretched ones are terrifying!
The King: Do not fear, long-lived ladies.
Viśvāmitra:
(Touching Rāma on the chin) My child, let her be slain.
Sītā: Alas! He himself is appointed to this very task here.
Rāma: Venerable sir, she is indeed a woman.
Ūrmilā: I am glad that the noble lady has said this.
Sītā:
(With wonder and affection) His change of heart is indeed directed toward something else entirely.
King: Well said; truly, the noble Rāma is a descendant of Ikṣvāku.
Rākṣasa: This is that Rāma, son of Daśaratha, who remained unshaken even at the sight of the violent assault of Tāṭakā, yet now hesitates when commanded to destroy her because she is a woman. (37)
Viśvāmitra: Hasten, my child! Do you not see before you this throng of Brahmins facing death?
Rāma: It is so; you gentlemen know this.
Because it is free from attachment to all defects, your consensus has attained the status of sacred tradition;
it is the authority regarding both merit and demerit. (38)
(Thus, having walked around, he exits.
Sītā: Alas! He has already departed. Woe, woe! Like a swarm of locusts, that wretched woman torments the noble-souled one.
The King, striking his bow: "Ah, you wicked woman! Stay! Stay!"
Ūrmilā: Oh, now Father has arrived here in person!
Lakṣmaṇa: (Smiling) Behold, sirs, Tāṭakā—
her limbs instantly breaking into convulsions from the impact of the fierce heron-feathered arrows that pierce the vital organs of the heart.
With streams of blood gushing forth from the two hollows of her nostrils like bubbles emerging from a cave, she was as if already dead. //39//
O maiden! A marvel, a marvel! A joy, a joy to us!
The King: Oh, how firm is the prince’s stroke!
Rākṣasa: Alas, noble Tāṭakā! What indeed can this mean? "Gourds sink in water, and stones float!
Truly, today the majesty of the Lord of Rākṣasas has faltered; today an unprecedented humiliation has been suffered at the hands of a mere human child.
I witnessed the slaughter of my own kin while standing by, and yet old age restrains me from acting as a messenger—what am I to do? (40)
Viśvāmitra: This, then, is the syllable Om.
Rākṣasa: Oh, sir! What answer do you have for us?
Viśvāmitra said:
"In this matter, Sīradhvaja is the one who knows [the truth], for Kuśadhvaja is indeed the younger.
He alone is the father of this maiden, the senior of the lineage, and the master."
The Rākṣasa said: "Both Kuśadhvaja and Viśvāmitra know this as well."
Viśvāmitra:
(To himself) This is the opportune moment to bestow the auspicious divine weapons; and the hour is indeed auspicious.

(Aloud: Friend Kuśadhvaja! By the grace of the venerable Kṛśāśva, through whom I have mastered the complete study of the divine weapon-mantras—including the secret applications and methods of withdrawal—by means of the vows and observances of a student, I shall now reveal to the noble Rāma the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the principles of those sciences, both in their meaning and their verbal form.

In ancient times, the primordial teachers, having performed austerities for more than a thousand autumns for the benefit of the Veda, beheld these very things as their own splendors composed of ascetic power. (42)
King: The Raghu lineage has been graced.
Lakṣmaṇa: By good fortune, there is the sound of celestial drums and a rain of flowers!
Rākṣasa: Ah! Even the denizens of heaven are acquiescing in what is hostile to the king!
Lakṣmaṇa: What?
How is it that the quarters of the sky appear as if suddenly drenched in molten, glowing gold due to their tawny hue, so that the day itself shines as if veiled by the twilight?
The heavens seem shrouded by a multitude of blazing banners and heaps of celestial weapons, appearing like a mass of lightning flickering incessantly, turning everything a golden-yellow. (43)

King: With his splendors blazing forth in every direction and surpassing the brilliance of the sun, my visual ray abandons its power, which is alternately seized and released in rapid succession. (44)
O maiden, with the radiance of their eyes flashing forth, they move about, enveloped on all sides by a mass of blazing, tawny-colored ignorance.

Rākṣasa: Oh, how difficult to withstand is the splendor of this divine weapon! By its very presence, I am reminded of the fury of the duel between Rāvaṇa and Purandara. Striking that chest which was directed with all his might by Indra, the fiercely radiant [weapon] shattered it into great fragments through the impact; thus, by its force, it turned the sky into a thunderbolt, while his master’s roars of rage and loud laughter became tawny with the flames from his mouth like thousands of lightning flashes. (45)

Viśvāmitra: O Rāmabhadra, pay homage to and take leave of these divine weapons—those which transcend Brahmā, Indra, Kubera, Rudra, Varuṇa, Prajāpati, the Maruts, Kāla, and Agni; which are the very essence of the Vedic mantras;
and whose power, like that of ascetic penances, is unsurpassed and exalted, such that the capacity of each one alone is sufficient to destroy or protect the three worlds. (46)
(Offstage:
"I am here, bowing before you, O Blessed One; and this is our request:
may this tradition of divine weapons be mine, together with Lakṣmaṇa. (47)
Viśvāmitra: O Rāmabhadra, so be it.
Lakṣmaṇa: Oh, what a grace!

Through the manifestation of this knowledge, I consider my own self to have suddenly blossomed with wisdom, beyond the reach of logical reasoning, and as if composed of light through its various powers. (48)
(Offstage:
O Rama, Rama, O mighty-armed one! We place ourselves under your protection;
by the command of Viśvāmitra, rule over us along with your brother. 49.
"O girl, the gods are speaking! Oh, what a marvel!"
(Offstage) O venerable hosts of divine weapons!
Having obtained you from Viśvāmitra, the friend of the universe, Rāma has today achieved his purpose through his merits.
Whenever you are meditated upon, you should manifest your presence; now go each to your own place. Salutations to you! (50)
Lakṣmaṇa: By the noble one's word, my weapons have been withdrawn.
The King: Blessed one, O great treasure of wonders, son of Kuśika, salutations to you!

Before you, a mass of splendor whose asceticism blazes and who possesses immeasurable power in this world, a speaker—who has dared to offer praise despite your boundless majesty—finds his capacity for expression limited; unable to find a place either in speech or in mind, his movement obstructed, he falters and is ashamed. (51)
Therefore, I envy Daśaratha, who is adorned by Rāmabhadra, whom you have favored. As for us, we have been deceived by my noble brother-in-law, since we are not united with such a son-in-law.
Viśvāmitra:
(Laughing) Why is this lack of confidence still directed toward us?
The King: Peace!
Viśvāmitra: Indeed, by that very means—may that bow of Śambhu, which grants its presence through mere meditation due to his boon, appear before the noble Rāma. (52)
The King: So be it.
(Reflecting, he bows.
Rākṣasa: (To himself: These men have introduced something quite different altogether.
(Aloud: O Kuśadhvaja, why do you deliberate so long?
The King said: "This has already been stated; the Noble One knows it."
The Rākṣasa replied, "This has already been answered; he too said that Kuśadhvaja knows."
The King said: "It is even so; Sīradhvaja knows this."
(From behind the scenes, following a tumultuous clamor:
A bow, as if fashioned from a thousand flashing thunderbolts, blazing with the splendor of the gods who brought an end to Tripura, appears before Rāma.
Sītā: Now I am truly reassured.
King: Just as an elephant with its trunk is placed upon a mountain peak by its young calf, so too has my staff-like arm been placed upon him.
Ūrmilā: Is it indeed possible that it should be so?
The King: [Having heard] the quality of the thundering and [seen] the furrowed [land], Ūrmilā—[embracing Sītā, who was both joyful and bashful]—says: "By good fortune, we prosper!"
The King: (With wonder) And it was shattered! //53//
Rākṣasa:
(To himself) Oh, how all-consuming is the power of that wretched Rāma!
The sound of the *ṭaṅkāra*— arising from his readiness to snap the staff-like bow of the moon-crested Lord with effortless ease of arm— is the drum signaling the prologue to the noble deeds of Bāla.

Alas, how is it that the massed ferocity of this [wind], which wanders within the belly of the vessel of the universe as its two halves suddenly meet like the joined lids of a pot, does not even now come to rest? //54//
The King: (As if with joy and madness) Come, come, dear child, delight of the Raghus, Rāmabhadra! I shall kiss you on the head and embrace you for a long time.
Or, having placed [you] in my heart, I carry you day and night; or else, I worship your two lotus-like feet. //55//
(Entering, Rāma: How is it that even transgression occurs out of excessive affection?
Viśvāmitra: You are my preceptor, and dear Rāmabhadra is your son in the form of an embryo.
The King: (Bowing) Venerable sir!
"By my husband Rāma, those blessings of yours were fulfilled for Sītā;
and on this very occasion, I have given Ūrmilā to Lakṣmaṇa. (56)
Girl!
(With tears) Oh, we are undone!
Rākṣasa: (To himself) That which was to be seen has been seen.
Viśvāmitra: We honor your words highly with our heads; however, there remains something yet to be said.
The King: Pray, give your command.
Viśvāmitra said: "I request your two daughters, Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti, for Bharata and Śatrughna."
Rākṛṣasa:
(To himself) Behold the audacity of this Brahmin, though he is but a forest-dweller, toward the family of a Kṣatriya!
The King: Blessed One, is there anything here that requires deliberation? However, in this matter, I am dependent on others.
Viśvāmitra: By whom?
The King: For one [offense], let it be by you alone.
Viśvāmitra said: "Then by whom else?"
The King: [It was] by the noble Sīradhvaja Gautama and by Śatānanda.
Viśvāmitra:
(Mockingly) I am the arbiter between Sīradhvaja and Śatānanda.
The King: Your Holiness now knows it;
to whom is the alliance between the Janakas and the Raghus not dear, wherein you, being of auspicious nature, are both the giver and the receiver? (57)

Viśvāmitra: Child Śunaḥśepha, go to Ayodhyā and speak these words of mine to the venerable Vasiṣṭha: "These four princesses, daughters of Nimi, have been given by me to these four descendants of Raghu, and accepted by them;
they were bestowed by me equally, having become like Vasiṣṭha and like Gautama. (58)

Having invited all those great seers, follow the great king Daśaratha and come to the city of Videha; for then, upon the completion of my sacrifice as well as that of the King of Mithilā, the princes, having performed the auspicious godāna ceremony, shall take their wives.
The princes: (To themselves) This is dearer than the dearest to us.
Daughter, by good fortune, there will now be no separation from your sisters.

Rākṣasa: O sirs, listen even now to a word of dharma! It is a misfortune for you that this maiden is to be given to another. You show no regard for this praiseworthy alliance, even though the descendant of Pulastya requests it with humility; nor do you have any desire for the happiness that comes from being the lord of the three worlds. Otherwise, Lankā itself will surely have to be abandoned by us along with Sītā. Therefore, let there not be for you here a fate like that which befell the city of Indra, where one becomes attached to a captive. (59)
(A confused noise behind the scenes. Princess:
Those two, as terrifying as untimely clouds, are rushing along with a great multitude.
Viśvāmitra: These two, Subāhu and Mārīca, are the sons of Sunda and Upasunda.
In the same way, let this obstacle to the sacrifice be struck down by you two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
"Let it be as you command."
(Thus they walk about with exaggerated gestures. Maidens! How shall we proceed here now?
Rākṣasa: Ah, this has turned out very well; the course of events must have been reversed.
Having observed the conclusion of the matter, I shall inform Mālyavat.
The King: (Stringing his bow) Dear Rāmabhadra, dear Lakṣmaṇa! Conquer the heedless one while remaining vigilant! Here I am, having arrived.
Viśvāmitra:
(Laughing and taking him by the hand) O King, come this way! Come!
Behold indeed the incomparable prowess of Rāma together with his younger brother;
for he destroys all enemies of the Brahmins, like a fierce Atharvan incantation of sorcery. //62//
(Thus they all exit. //The First Act//
